turns.zh: 好的。我在一家名为Simon-Kucher的咨询公司担任高级合伙人。我们是全球最大的定价策略咨询公司，在全球43个办事处拥有约2000名员工。我在湾区办事处工作，已有15年从业经验，主要为湾区科技公司提供服务，包括软件公司、互联网市场平台等领域。我们与250多家公司合作，其中20多家独角兽企业涉及定价、变现、盈利增长等领域。比如Uber、Asana、DoorDash、LinkedIn等知名企业都与我们有过合作。您之前提到我撰写的《创新变现》一书，确实售出了不少副本。（00:04:56）刚开始推广这本书时，我们会追踪销量数据，但很快意识到书籍的价值在于能产生实际影响。这也是我们写作的初衷。衡量《创新变现》影响力的标准，是每天都有读者联系我们，表示通过阅读本书在公司定价与变现方面取得了成效。对我而言，这才是真正的价值所在，也是我持续创作的动力。我们写作时并不想堆砌营销辞藻，而是致力于提供可操作的实践方案。看到读者能将其应用于实际工作，推动企业变革，这才是真正的意义。当然，这本书反响热烈。例如，在亚马逊多个分类榜单上始终位列前十，至今已出版六年。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: I actually happened to stumble in it. It's classic fashion. I was at Stanford Graduate School, both Graduate School of Business and the Engineering School. And we had a lot of startup discussions thinking of creating startup, very classic. How do you truly know? And I was like, oh, I actually don't. I just made stuff up. And within that same week I got a call from the then managing partner of Simon-Kucher, Matt Johnson. (00:07:27): And he said, hey, we're starting a pricing and growth strategy consulting firm. You want to come join us? We're looking for Stanford grads and I was like, whoa, I didn't even know you existed. I joined because I actually wanted to get to understand the science behind pricing, not just the art. And that's what I've been focusing on in the last 15 years. And also my education in Stanford was in quantitative marketing. So many of those, let's say theoretical models I could bring back into a practical industry in a relevant sense. So it's been a great journey.
turns.zh: 实际上，我是偶然接触到这个领域的。这很符合典型创业者的经历。我曾就读于斯坦福大学商学院和工程学院。我们经常讨论创业项目，构思商业计划书，这很常见。当我们向风险投资公司推销项目时，我负责制定定价变现策略。记得当时VC问我：你怎么知道这项创新能盈利？我拿出电子表格，展示所有假设条件，回答说：我就要这么做。结果他说：你得把这些假设调整过来。你怎么能确定呢？我说：哦，我其实并不能确定，都是随便编的。结果当周，Simon-Kucher公司的当时管理合伙人Matt Johnson给我打电话：我们要创办一家定价与增长策略咨询公司，你想加入吗？我们正在寻找斯坦福校友。我说：哇，我都不知道你们有这家公司。我加入是因为我想深入理解定价背后的科学逻辑，而不只是停留在艺术层面。过去15年我一直专注于此。我的斯坦福教育背景也是定量营销，所以很多理论模型都能结合实际行业应用。这是一段很棒的旅程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I think about books that people find most useful and sustain or books that are based on people's real experience doing a thing for a decade, and your book is a great example that, what made you decide to actually write a book? Because I know how hard that is from my wife's experience.
turns.zh: 谈到人们觉得最有用的书，或者基于真实经验写的书，比如你这本。是什么促使你决定写这本书？因为从我妻子的经历来看，我知道这有多难。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah, I think it probably started with some mini frustration, because we used to get calls from companies saying, hey, we need a pricing strategy, we need a price plan. And they would've invested years probably making the innovation. And then we'd ask them, how long do we have? And they're like, we need it yesterday. So time and again, we witnessed this spray and pray approach. And then we used to ask this simple question, how do you truly know that people will actually pay for your innovation, when you built it? Did you do any studies? Did you actually understand whether there's a product market pricing fit? And usually the answer was no. And then it had to change. When we benchmarked 72% of innovations actually fail from a monetization or commercial perspective, simply because entrepreneurs or companies did not do the check earlier on. Had they done it, they could have probably pivoted the product, built things in a different way and built something that was more meaningful. (00:09:17): So we wrote Monetizing Innovation because increasingly we were working with companies more early stage in helping them design the right innovations that customers need and what are they willing to pay for, as opposed to just building a product and slapping on a price. So it was crossing that chasm between knowing and hoping that you would, monetize knowing that you truly will. And that was the motivation for writing Monetizing Innovation.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得最初可能是因为一些小挫折。比如公司打电话来说：我们需要定价策略，需要价格规划方案。他们可能已经投入数年打造创新成果了。然后我们问：你们还有多久时间？他们说：昨天就要。一次又一次，我们目睹这种“盲目尝试”的做法。接着我们会问一个简单问题：当你们开发出创新成果后，怎么确定人们愿意为此付费？你们做过研究吗？你们了解产品与市场的价格匹配度吗？通常答案都是否定的。这时候必须改变现状。我们发现72%的创新项目从变现或商业化角度失败，仅仅因为创业者或公司没有提前验证。如果他们早点验证，或许就能调整产品方向，采用不同的构建方式，打造更有价值的东西。（00:09:17）所以我们写了《定价创新》这本书，因为我们越来越多地与早期阶段的公司合作，帮助他们设计真正满足客户需求、且客户愿意为之付费的创新项目，而不是简单地构建产品然后随便定价。这本书就是要跨越从“希望创新能变现”到“确信创新一定能变现”的鸿沟。这就是我们写《定价创新》的初衷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to dive into a lot of these things that you've shared in the book and things you've learned. One more context setting question before we get into it all, which part of the org do you believe pricing strategies should sit in? Is it product sales, finance, marketing, something else?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们接下来要深入探讨你书中提到的诸多内容，以及你积累的经验。在深入之前，我想先问一个背景性问题：你认为定价策略应该归属于组织中的哪个部门？是产品部门、财务部门、市场部门，还是其他部门？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Pricing by discipline is a cross-functional discipline. You can't talk pricing in isolation of product, finance, sales, et cetera. There's always touch points. So it's extremely cross-functional. Back in the day, probably a decade ago, I used to say pricing needs to sit in finance, because my view was finance would be the counterbalance to sales, especially if you have sales coming up with pricing in a B2B situation, you can set all the pricing you want, it's human having a human conversation. So how do you put checks and balance in some of that? And my view was pricing should sit in finance and it has to report on ultimately to the CFO. I have, over the last decade, I've been actually advocating that they should sit in the product side. (00:10:40): And there was also the genesis of Monetizing Innovation because if we truly believe that we need to build products that are simply products that customers need, they love, they value, they're willing to pay for, it is a product function, because you need to be able to design the product around this information, around what customers need, what they value, and what they're willing to pay for, in short, around the price. If you look at Monetizing Innovation, the subtitle of the book is, How Smart Companies Design Their Products Around the Price. So if you take that viewpoint, then pricing needs to sit in the product function or the founder product and report onto this. This is my strong-held belief, one that probably won't change now.
turns.zh:
定价本质上是跨职能的工作。你不可能孤立地谈论定价，而忽视产品、财务、销售等部门。它们之间总是存在交集。因此，定价策略的制定极具跨职能性。十年前，我曾主张定价应归属于财务部门，因为财务部门可以平衡销售部门的诉求。尤其是在B2B场景下，当销售部门提出定价方案时，财务部门需要对其进行把关。但近十年来，我逐渐转变观点，认为定价应归属于产品部门。（00:10:40）  
《创新变现》的诞生也源于此——如果我们坚信产品必须满足客户需求、赢得客户喜爱、创造价值并获得付费意愿，那么定价策略就必须与产品职能紧密结合。毕竟，产品设计必须围绕客户需求、价值认知和支付意愿展开，最终以定价为核心。正如《创新变现》副标题所言——“聪明的公司如何围绕定价设计产品”。从这个角度看，定价策略应归属于产品部门或创始人团队，并向其汇报。这是我坚信不移的观点，不太可能轻易改变。

So most of the listeners of this podcast are product builders and people that grow, product managers, founders, people that work on cross-functional product teams. And I was reading a book and I picked five topics that I thought would be especially useful to product leaders to dig into.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这为我们的深入探讨提供了绝佳契机。听众中多数是产品开发者、产品经理、创始人以及跨职能产品团队成员。我在阅读这本书时，挑选了五个对产品领导者特别有价值的主题进行深度探讨。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the first is the, willingness to pay, conversations. Which I know is foundational to the way that you think about pricing strategy and the advice that you share with people of how to think about pricing. So can you just talk about, just what is willingness to pay as a concept? And then when should founders focus on these conversations to figure out the willingness to pay?
turns.zh: 第一个主题是支付意愿的对话。我知道这是你思考定价策略的基础，也是你为人们提供定价思路的核心建议。能否请你先解释一下“支付意愿”这个概念？然后创始人何时应该关注这些对话以深入理解客户的支付意愿？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So I think, look, most of your listeners, most product folks, they probably understand language like product market fit, especially made famous from lead startup and other literature, which is awesome. I think that the issue is, it's not just about product market fit, it is about achieving a product market pricing fit. For instance, if someone comes and asks me, do you like the headset that you're using for this podcast? I'll say, I like it. Do you like it at $200? The whole conversation is different. So if you didn't put pricing as part of your product market fit validation, you're often hearing what you want to hear. It is truly about understanding whether customers are willing to pay for your innovation and willingness to pay is a proxy for, do people actually value your product? And how badly do they actually want the product? (00:12:56): And this even comes back to understanding what pricing really is. When we talk about pricing, many people quickly gravitate to dollar figures. That's just a price point, that's a dollar figure. But when we think about price, we think about it as a measure. Like liter is a measure of volume, price is a measure of value. And when you think of it this way, it really stands for, do people actually want your product and would they actually buy it? And that is their whole, willingness to pay conversation. And entrepreneurs and companies need to do this much earlier, so that they can understand, are they on the right track? Think of it this way, if I have the same sales and marketing conversation that I would have with the customer six months before launch of the product, pitch the whole value, and then ask them a simple question, would you pay for this innovation? And if someone says no, chances are you can put all the [inaudible 00:13:47] you want in the next six months, they're going to say the same thing. (00:13:49): And if they do say no, the most important question to ask is why. And you start hearing all kinds of information that you can use to design your product and maybe even pivot your product strategy accordingly. So it is literally the litmus test of whether people like your product.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对正确。我认为，大多数听众，尤其是产品从业者，应该都熟悉“产品市场契合度”这样的概念——这个术语最初由“领头羊创业公司”（LeadStartup）等文献推广，确实很有启发意义。但问题在于，产品市场契合度不只是指产品与市场的匹配，还包括实现产品与市场价格的契合。比如，如果有人问我：“你喜欢用于这期播客的耳机吗？”我会回答：“我喜欢。”但如果他们接着问：“你愿意花200美元买它吗？”整个对话的重点就完全不同了。如果在验证产品市场契合度时忽略了价格因素，你很可能只听到自己想听的答案。真正关键的是，要了解客户是否愿意为你的创新买单，而这种意愿恰恰反映了他们对产品的价值认可程度，以及他们对产品的迫切需求。（00:12:56）这甚至关乎对价格本质的理解。当我们谈论定价时，许多人往往只关注数字本身。这只是一个价格标签，但从本质上讲，价格是价值的衡量标准。换句话说，价格实际上是在衡量用户对产品的需求和购买意愿。这才是他们愿意为产品付费的核心逻辑。创业者和企业需要尽早关注这一点，以便判断自己的方向是否正确。举个例子，如果你在产品上线前六个月，与客户进行同样的销售和市场沟通，全面展示产品的价值，然后简单问一句：“你愿意为这项创新付费吗？”如果对方回答“不愿意”，未来六个月无论你投入多少精力（00:13:47），他们的答案都可能一样。（00:13:49）如果他们确实拒绝，最关键的问题是：“为什么？”这样你就能收集到大量有价值的信息，用于产品设计，甚至调整策略。这简直是验证用户是否喜欢你的产品的试金石。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so if I were to summarize your main point, the ideas, have these conversations right as you're thinking about designing the product. Don't try to just launch it, see how people like it, build a huge audience and then figure out pricing. Your advice is start having those conversations early, right?
turns.zh: 所以如果要总结你的核心观点，那就是在设计产品时就应该尽早开展这些对话。不要等到产品上线后才去观察用户反馈，再调整价格策略。你的建议是尽早开启这些对话，对吧？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Exactly. And the folks that first round summarized this in four words, I thought when they wrote a blog article on this, and they call it, price before product, period. So I think that probably succinct, but really it's really that. Because frankly, Lenny, as an entrepreneur, a company, you actually don't have a choice whether you'll have a pricing conversation with your customer. The only thing in your control is when you will have it. You can build the most awesome innovation, you think is awesome, obsess over the engineering, the product and everything else, and then slap on a price [inaudible 00:14:55] in the market and hope to monetize or have this conversation much earlier, pitch the same sales and marketing pitches, and then try to understand whether people will actually pay for it and then design around this information. And you actually know that you will. So you're maximizing your chances for success. It's simply testing and learning. Everyone in your probably listener base knows tests and learn. We are talking about testing and learning pricing and willingness to pay. Why wouldn't you do that? And why would you postpone that to the very end?
turns.zh: 确实如此。那些在第一轮用四个词总结这一点的人——我记得他们写了一篇关于这个的博客文章——他们称之为"先定价，后做产品，仅此而已"。我觉得这说得简洁明了，但本质上就是这个道理。说实话，莱尼，作为一名创业者或企业主，你实际上无法选择是否要和客户谈论定价问题。你唯一能控制的是何时开启这个对话。你可以开发出你自认为很棒的创新产品，沉迷于工程设计、产品研发等各个环节，然后在市场上随便定个价格[00:14:55语音不清]，指望能变现或尽早开启这个对话，用同样的销售和营销策略去试探用户是否愿意为此买单，再根据反馈进行产品设计。但你明明知道自己必须这么做，这样才能最大化成功几率。这不过是不断测试与学习的过程。想必听众中很多人都熟悉测试与学习的理念。我们今天讨论的是如何测试定价策略和用户支付意愿。为什么不这么做呢？又为什么要把这件事拖到最后一刻呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any examples of products or companies where they have these conversations either way too early, way too late, or even just nailed it?
turns.zh: 你能否举一些产品或公司的例子，说明他们在定价对话上是过早、过晚进行的，甚至是处理得非常到位的？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Here's the thing, there's nothing way too early for this conversation. I even tell people who are early C-stage or just thinking about an idea, I would say, hey, go check, so if someone would actually pay for this idea. And there's some high level ways to actually check for this. And of course there's not about nailing the pricing strategy from get-go, three years before a product is launched, et cetera. It's about understanding whether there is a willingness to pay and then repeating this exercise as you go along so that you can refine and when you're ready to launch the product, you have a much more refined view on what is the willingness to pay. And of course then you're launching the product with a lot more enthusiasm, because you know this is actually going to have a product market pricing fit. So it's about iterating and learning and refining. (00:16:15): So there's never too early. Too late, I think is more so the companies, this is why we wrote Monetizing Innovation. Like I told you. 72% of innovations fail and we also categorize them into why they fail. There are only four failure types and I have written about that in the book, so I can leave that for readers to actually go and see it. But all of those failure types happen because the conversation was just too late and pricing was an afterthought. Companies that did it well, maybe one or two examples that I can probably take just to motivate the concept, we talk about in the first chapter a tale of two cars and about how Porsche actually did this. And the example is something like this relevant, Porsche was really looking for launching a new innovation. They came up with an idea. They said, okay, should we launch an SUV? (00:17:05): And even before a blueprint was drawn, they basically went and checked with the market, is there a need for an SUV? Would people value it from Porsche? Are they willing to pay for it? And to their surprise, they actually found that. And then what they did next was more fascinating. Every single feature that actually went into the car or the benefit that people had, was battle-tested with customers and no amount of convincing from product or engineering was enough. It had to be battle-tested with customers. Things like, for instance, big cup holder was inside because people loved it, needed an SUV would pay for it. Things like six feet manual transmission. People didn't need an SUVs out of the window. They literally used to bring cars in what is called as car clinics. And they would test for this and they would put people through prototypes before anything is even productized, anything is in the factory floor, where people would actually even drive around the Porsche and say, okay, did they like it? Would they pay for it? Et cetera. (00:18:05): And then they would fine tune everything as thing that goes on. So the innovation process is very different from the classic spray and pray, build something, slap on a price, throw it out. It was really designing the product around customer feedback, around willingness to pay. The outcome of the process could also couldn't have been more different than the traditional approach of spray and pray. And this was when they launched this SUV, it was called Cayenne, which we all know now, and it accounts for more than half of Porsche's profit and literally one of the best rolling successes in automotive history. There's just an automotive example, but if I switch gears to more of a tech example or a software example for your audience, there was this company which, think of this as a two-sided marketplace, and I'll just keep it a bit abstract, but I'll tell you the details. (00:18:56): Two-sided marketplace, think of this as they were already monetizing on the sell side and the CEO said, okay, let's go and build a product for the buy side that people will buy. So the buy side monetization product strategy. So in classic fashion, all the product folks, product managers, et cetera, they went offsite, generated thousands of post-it notes, design thinking, yada yada, everything. And then they said, okay, we can't take all of these so many ideas to the CEO, let's prioritize it somehow. And they prioritized it to 40 ideas and they took it to the CEO and said, this is what we want to build. And the CEO asked a simple question, how do you truly know you would monetize? It's the same question the VC asked me, back in the day, and they simply didn't know. They were just guessing. So what happened next was they took wire frames, blueprints, they took product concepts and they started testing this with their customers and prospects. (00:19:55): So stuff that they actually thought was exciting, often was way down in the list of priorities. And if they didn't do these kind of tests, they would've probably built the product around this. To give you an example, one of the features that they were building was called, or the number one feature that the internal team thought was awesome, they called it Highlight Connections from Facebook. And everyone in the company thought that people would pay for this. It's an awesome feature, they need it, they love it. And the thesis was something like this. As a buyer, if I'm buying the product from the same seller and someone in my Facebook connection has already bought that product from that seller, that's credible information in lieu of reviews and everything else, and people would find it acceptable and pay for this. When they went and tested this and pitched the idea, they got all kinds of reactions. (00:20:47): So there was one customer group I remember which said, so yeah, you're telling me I can't pull 200 of reviews and make my own determination? That's unacceptable. That spoils the fun out of actually doing research on products. There was another group of customers who said, do you like it? Yeah, I like it. Would you pay for it? Hell no. And then there was another group which even said, I don't even want anyone in my Facebook circle to know that I'm buying this product. Because there was some, let's say, premiumness associated with this and everything else. They could not find a single set of customers or a segment of customers who said, I love this feature, I would pay for it. If they hadn't done this exercise, they would've built the entire product around this and it would've been a disaster. But because they actually did this, they could prioritize what they were building. (00:21:36): Literally, for your product folks, the number one lesson, and I hope this is the biggest takeaway for your audience, you cannot prioritize a product roadmap without having a willingness to pay conversation. If you're just prioritizing based on what you think or what you feel or technical resources, you're getting it wrong. Literally, you can prioritize what you are building based on what customers need, what they value, and what they're willing to pay for. And you can actually do this test and say, what should you be building? The funny thing that I've actually always seen, always, across these hundreds of companies that I've worked, 20% of what you build drives 80% of the willingness to pay, is a classic burrito. And if you don't know this, you're probably all indexing on one or the other. It's much better to find out what is this 20% so that you can focus on it, nail it, and focus on all of the usability around it and make an awesome product as opposed to not knowing what drives the willingness to pay and just trying to put everything out there. (00:22:38): And at the worst form, often what happens then is this 20% is the easiest thing to build. And what companies do is they will build it, they will throw it out and they'll say, there's an MVP, give it for free. And then they're trying to chase their tails, building 80% of stuff that is driving 20% of value. So you all already lost the battle. So as a product person or a product builder, you need to prioritize your R&D roadmap based on willingness to pay conversations, exactly like what the two-sided marketplace did, exactly like what Porsche did. And this is the crux of everything that we are talking about.
turns.zh:
关键在于，开始这场对话永远不嫌早。我甚至会对那些处于C阶段初期或只是构思创意的人说：去验证一下，看看是否真有人愿意为这个想法买单。验证用户意愿的方法有很多种，当然这不意味着要在产品发布前三年就敲定定价策略。关键在于了解用户的支付意愿，然后在产品上线前不断迭代优化。这样一来，当产品真正推向市场时，你对用户支付意愿的把握就会更加精准，推向市场的信心也会更足。

（00:16:15）所以永远不嫌早。但我认为真正的“太晚”往往出现在企业层面。这正是我们写《创新变现》一书的原因。正如我之前提到的，72%的创新项目以失败告终。我们对失败原因进行了分类，归纳出四种失败类型，相关内容在书中均有详述，感兴趣的读者可以去查阅。但所有失败案例的根源都在于对用户需求的洞察过晚，以及定价被视为事后之想。那些成功的案例，比如我们在第一章提到的保时捷SUV项目，堪称典范。保时捷在构思新品时，就开始通过市场调研验证用户需求：是否有SUV市场需求？保时捷的SUV能否被认可？用户是否愿意为此买单？令人惊喜的是，他们发现了巨大的市场潜力。

（00:17:05）接下来，保时捷将每一项产品功能都进行了用户测试。无论是大容量杯架、6速手动变速箱等细节，都经过了客户验证。没有任何工程或产品部门的强行说服，所有决策都基于真实用户反馈。比如，用户认为6速手动变速箱实用，愿意为此付费。保时捷甚至邀请用户参与“汽车诊所”活动，亲自试驾新车并反馈体验。

（00:18:05）整个创新过程与传统的“撞大运、快速上线、定价后再优化”的模式截然不同。保时捷围绕用户需求和支付意愿进行产品设计，最终成果远超传统的碰运气式创新。推向市场的SUV——卡宴，如今占据保时捷利润的半壁江山，成为汽车史上最成功的车型之一。这只是一个汽车领域的案例，但若转向科技或软件领域，同样有值得借鉴的范例。比如某两面市场的平台公司，其成功之路同样依赖于对用户需求的精准洞察。
接下来我会讲得稍微抽象一些，但具体细节我会告诉你的。（00:18:56）：双边市场平台。假设他们已经在卖方端实现了变现，CEO说好，我们去为买方端开发一个产品，让人们愿意购买。这就是买方端变现的产品策略。按照惯例，所有产品团队成员、产品经理等等都出去开会，写了上千张便利贴，进行设计思维之类的讨论。但最后他们说，我们不能把所有这些想法都带给CEO，还是得优先排序吧。他们筛选出了40个想法，带去给CEO，说这就是我们想做的。CEO问了一个简单的问题：你们怎么知道这些能变现？这和VC当初问我的问题如出一辙，他们根本不知道，只是猜测。接下来他们拿出线框图、蓝图，展示产品概念，开始向客户和潜在用户测试。（00:19:55）：结果那些他们自以为很棒的功能，往往在优先级列表里排得很低。如果不做这些测试，他们很可能就围绕这些功能来开发产品了。举个例子，他们正在开发的一个功能，内部团队认为最棒的，叫“Facebook好友关系突出显示”。公司上下都觉得人们会为此付费。这是个很棒的功能，用户需要它，爱它。他们的设想是这样的：作为买家，如果我从同一个卖家那里购买产品，而我的Facebook好友已经从这个卖家那里买过同款产品，这就是比评论更有价值的信任信息，人们会愿意为此付费。但测试结果令人意外。（00:20:47）：有个客户群体说，你是说我不能自己收集200条评论来做决策吗？这太不合理了，会破坏用户自主研究产品的乐趣。另一个客户群体说，你喜欢这个功能？是的，我喜欢。但你会为此付费？绝对不愿意。还有个群体甚至说，我不想让Facebook好友知道我在买这个产品。这里有种所谓的身份高贵感之类的东西。他们找不到任何愿意为此付费的客户群体或细分市场。如果当初不做测试，他们很可能就围绕这个功能来开发整个产品，那将是一场灾难。但正因为他们做了测试，才能合理排序。（00:21:36）：对产品团队来说，最重要的经验教训——我希望这也是听众最大的收获——就是在排序产品路线图之前，必须先进行付费意愿对话。如果只是根据个人判断、感觉或技术资源来排序，那就错了。必须根据客户需求、价值和付费意愿来排序。通过测试你才能知道应该开发什么功能。我见过很多公司，20%的开发成果能带来80%的付费意愿，这就是典型的墨守成规。还有，如果你
可能很多人都不清楚这一点，但你们很可能都在盲目开发产品功能。更明智的做法是，先搞清楚那20%的核心价值所在，这样你才能专注于此，精心打磨，并围绕它优化整个用户体验，最终打造出卓越的产品，而不是在不了解用户支付意愿的前提下，一股脑地堆砌功能。（00:22:38）最糟糕的情况是，开发团队往往会把这20%的核心功能当作最容易实现的部分。很多公司会快速开发出来，然后随意推向市场，声称这是个最小可行产品（MVP），免费提供。结果他们却陷入了死循环，费力开发占据80%资源的功能，却只获取了20%的价值。这样一来，产品团队就已经输在了起跑线上。作为产品经理或开发者，必须根据用户支付意愿来规划研发路线图，就像双边市场平台那样做的，就像保时捷这样的品牌所做的那样。这才是我们所讨论的核心要义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What's interesting about the second example versus the first is in the Porsche example, they started with, we want to charge this much. Let's build a car that we can sell for that much. And the second case, they had a product they were trying to build, and then they figured out which things to build. So it's interesting that this can come along the journey at different places, but the main takeaway is do it early and earlier than you think.
turns.zh: 太棒了。第二个例子和第一个例子的有趣之处在于，在保时捷的案例中，他们首先设定了一个价格目标——“我们想定价这么高”，然后再据此打造一款能以该价格售出的汽车。而第二个案例中，他们先有了一款产品，再根据市场需求确定优先开发的功能。这说明，类似的思考路径在产品开发的不同阶段可能出现，但核心要义是尽早行动，行动得比你想象的更早。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Correct. Either productize to a price point and the willingness to pay, or at least use willingness to pay as an access to prioritize what you're building. Either way, you'll get it right.
turns.zh: 没错。要么根据目标价格和客户支付意愿进行产品化，要么至少以客户支付意愿为依据来确定优先开发的功能。无论哪种方式，最终都能找到正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let's actually talk about how to have these conversations. I imagine that's what a lot of people are wondering right now. It's like, yes, I'm convinced I will have these conversations, but then the classic issue with customers, you ask them what they all do and you can't trust their stories of what they'll actually do. So what advice do you have for folks when they have these conversations? What questions should they ask? What words should they use? I know you have a few frameworks that you suggest, you can talk about that.

turns.en: The first one is, what we say is, "Frame the question in a more relative manner", because, and sometimes I say tongue in cheek, that, "People are absolutely meaningless, relatively super smart." What I mean by that is, if you go and ask someone, "How much should I charge?" You'll get a meaningless answer. But if you actually ask it in a relative way, people actually give responses that are meaningful. So for instance, if you're a B2B SaaS company, and you're trying to see if your product actually has willingness to pay, one way to have that conversation is to say, "Okay. Hey, do your customers, do you use products like Salesforce in your install base?" "Yeah, I do use." "Okay, Salesforce was indexed at 100 in value. Where do you think we are in terms of the value that we bring to your, let's say, day to day business operations?" That people can answer all day long. (00:25:49): They might say, "80", they might say, "120", depending on whether you're more or less compared to, let's say, what a Salesforce can do, which is an established [inaudible 00:25:56]. And then if you say, "Okay, if Salesforce was indexed at a 100 in pricing, where do you think we should be?" That also people can say, okay, if they say 110, what they're saying is, you can be more premium than that and we would still pay for it. At least you've gotten some information that is meaningful at a very basic level. So this is some relative ways of asking these questions are the most basic ways of actually doing it. (00:26:18): Then we have questions where there's some methods where we actually want to understand, are there some psychological thresholds or budgets when it comes to willingness to pay? So the way to do this is let's take your product that you're going to launch, pitch the value to your customers, have that exact sales and marketing conversation that you'd have after you launch the product, but before. And then you ask them, "What do you think is an acceptable price for this innovation?" Look, everyone would like to low ball, they'll negotiate with themselves. Let them give an answer, clock it, then ask them, "What do you think is an expensive price?" And then follow that with, "What do you think is a prohibitively expensive price?" And across thousands of projects that we have done, what we have come to realize is, acceptable price is the price where people not only love the product, but they also love the price. If you're in true growth mode, maybe you can put it there as a no-brainer price, no friction, et cetera. The expensive price tends to be the price that is value priced, as in, they don't love you, they don't hate you, they would pay you, but that's a neutral reaction. Prohibitively expensive tends to be the price that they'll laugh you out the room. And if you do this at scale, what you'll start seeing is that there are some cliffs in these demand curves, where suddenly, when you cross from let's say 99 to 101, 20 or 30% might say, "It is expensive," or, "Hey, it's prohibitively expensive." (00:27:42): And that's what we look for to see if there are some psychological thresholds that if you actually cross, you have a perception of being expensive. So hiding behind some of these psychological thresholds become important. Rahul Vohra from Superhuman actually read the book, and he talked about this in an a16z podcast. He actually used this method to come up with his $30 price point for the Superhuman app. And I think that's a quick and dirty way to actually get to, what is a willingness to pay, and what's a psychological threshold? So I think that's a interesting method that you can do Monday morning. (00:28:16): But the key here is to not just ask the question, "What would you pay?" But have that sales and marketing conversation. Tell people where they actually might get the benefits. Basically, exactly everything you would do after launching the product to create awareness and showcase the benefits, do it, and then ask these questions, so that you're priming them to the value that your product gets and you're not just having a random conversation. There are other techniques that go more and more, let's say, rigorous. For instance, purchase probability questions. So if you ask someone, "Okay, would you buy this product?" That's a meaningless question. At least if you ground them on a scale and say, "On a scale of one to five, would you buy it?" One is, "I'm not at all interested", five is, "Most likely I would buy it," or, "I would buy it for certain." And four is, "Most likely", for instance, and three is, "I'm neutral." (00:29:06): What we are actually seeing is, even if people say, "Five", they are probably only 30 to 50% sure about whether they would buy, so you can start, and if they say, "Four", it's 10 to 20%. If they say, "Three and below", they're never going to buy it. (00:29:20): So if you do this at scale, you can start coming up with, let's say a demand curve. And then say, "Where is the price optimal?" et cetera. So you can understand purchase probabilities. And if someone says, let's say, three, for a certain price point, then you can lower the price and say, okay, would they actually move their ratings to a four or five. So I think these are some simple ways to understand purchase probabilities and elasticities. Two more, if I may, I think, another one is what we call is most and least questions. And the thesis behind this is, if you go and ask people, "Okay, I give them a list of 10 features", let's say. And I say, "Rank them one to 10", most people will find that exercise painful, horrible, because there's always this messy middle where everything is gray. They all look the same. (00:30:06): There's a lot of psychological theory that people are very adept at identifying the extremes. When it gets in the between, that's when things become tougher. So what we do is, if we have a list of 10 features that we want to understand whether people have willingness to pay for, when we are prioritizing the R&D roadmap for our clients, we would take a subset of, let's say six or so features out of those 10. And then they say, "In this set of features, identify the most important for you, and the least important." And the most important is defined as, "Must have, I will pay for it." Least important is, "I don't need it. I won't pay for it", connotation. This, people can do all day long, because they're just picking the two. And then we will change the set of six, another combination from the 10, and ask that same question. (00:30:49): So if you do this a few times, you will be able to prioritize the entire feature set in a relative fashion, and truly understand what drives willingness to pay. The last method, which gets into more advanced methodology, is what we call is more trade-off exercises. So here, what we do is we put people through actual buying patterns, or actual buying scenarios and say, "Okay, if you had this packaging and pricing, for instance, for your software product, what would you do?" Which is akin to a real life question. You [inaudible 00:31:19] the features, all the price, the number of plans, et cetera. (00:31:21): Then we would change that and say, "Okay. If you change the features and the price, how would you react? Would you buy any of these products? Or would you say, I won't choose any of these?" These are more like shopping scenarios for your products, but it's realistic, and it's akin to real life. Based on how they choose these products, what we are trying to reveal is the mental models and rules that people use to make decisions. So for instance, if I add certain amount of features and increase the price, people say, "You know what? I'm not going to buy anything more." (00:31:50): What that actually tells you is the addition of those features, people are not willing to pay the addition in terms of price, so they would actually opt out of the lineup that you actually have for your customers. So these kind of things, if you do these kind of exercise, you can get more precise on things like price elasticity, build some simulation models, try to understand how the market would react, et cetera. And different methods are actually applicable at different stages of a product and different stages of a company. If you're very early stage, let's say just an idea, just have the conversation. Just even asking, would you pay for it, is a good question because if someone says no, then ask why. (00:32:29): Then you'll hear a lot of good information. If someone says yes, ask them, why would you pay for it, they would articulate back the value that they understood, and that should be in your value messaging. So that's just the simple questions. If you are somewhere in middle, then maybe some of these, if you're in the [inaudible 00:32:44] seat stage, maybe some of the purchase property questions, all of these things can actually be a quick and dirty way to at least get to an answer and a point of view. Or if you're launching a product and it's in late stage or late stage in the product or the company lifecycle, and you need to get more precise in terms of your pricing and packaging strategy, then some of the methods are around trade off exercises, most, least, all of these things become incredibly relevant. Sorry, it was a long answer, but there are so many methods. It's all summarized in chapter four. So just one chapter to read in the book.

首先，我们要说的是，“用更相对的方式来设定问题”，因为有时候我会开玩笑地说，“人其实完全没有意义，但相对来说却超级聪明。”我的意思是，如果你去问某人：“我该收多少钱？”你会得到一个毫无意义的答案。但如果你用相对的方式提问，人们给出的回答才会富有意义。举个例子，如果你是一家B2B SaaS公司，想要了解客户是否愿意为你的产品付费，一种有效的沟通方式是：“好的，你们的客户中，有用过Salesforce这类产品的吗？”  “是的，我用过。”  “好的，Salesforce的价值被设定为100分，你觉得我们能为你的日常业务运营带来多少价值呢？” 这样人们就能畅谈一天了。（00:25:49）他们可能会说80分，或者120分，这取决于你与Salesforce的比较程度——毕竟Salesforce是一个成熟的平台[00:25:56，原文不清]。然后你再问：“好的，如果Salesforce的定价被设定为100分，你们觉得我们应该定多少呢？” 这样人们就能给出答案，比如110分。这意味着他们认为你的产品可以比Salesforce更贵，而用户仍愿意为此付费。至少你获得了最基础层面的有意义信息。这些相对提问方式是实际操作中最基础的做法。（00:26:18）接下来是更深层的探索：客户在支付意愿方面是否存在心理门槛或预算限制？方法是提前推出即将上线的产品，向客户传递价值主张，进行产品上线前的销售与营销对话。然后你问他们：“你们认为这个创新产品的合理价格是多少？” （大家都想压低价格，会自我博弈）记录他们的答案，再追问：“你们觉得这个价格算贵吗？” 最后再问：“你们觉得这个价格太贵了吗？” 通过数千个项目实践，我们发现：合理价格是客户既爱产品又爱价格的点；贵的价格是价值匹配型定价，用户不爱不恨，愿意支付；太贵的价格则让用户嘲笑离场。大规模应用这些方法后，需求曲线会出现断崖式变化——比如从99到101，20%-30%的用户会认为“太贵了”或“贵得离谱”。这些心理门槛的识别至关重要。Superhuman的Rahul Vohra读过这本书，并在a16z播客中分享了这种方法。他用此法为Superhuman应用设定了30美元的定价点。我认为这是一种快速直观的获取支付意愿和心理门槛的方法。
一个你可以在周一早上尝试的有趣方法。（00:28:16）：但关键在于，不要只是问“你愿意为此付多少钱？”，而是要进行销售和营销对话。告诉人们他们实际上能获得哪些好处。基本上，你在产品发布后用于创造认知和展示优势的所有步骤，都可以提前实施，然后再提出这些问题，这样就能让用户对产品的价值产生预期，而不仅仅是随意交谈。还有更深入的技巧，比如购买概率问题。比如，如果你问某人“好的，你会购买这款产品吗？”这是一个毫无意义的问题。至少你需要给出一个量化标准，比如“1到5分，你会购买吗？”1分表示“完全不感兴趣”，5分表示“极有可能购买”，或者“肯定会购买”。4分表示“很有可能购买”，3分表示“持中立态度”。（00:29:06）：我们实际观察到，即使有人说自己会给5分，他们对购买的确定性也只有30%到50%。所以你可以从这个量化结果入手，构建需求曲线，然后问“价格最优点在哪里？”等等。这样就能了解购买概率。如果有人说某个价格点的评分是3分，你可以降低价格，再问他们是否会将评分提升到4分或5分。我认为这些都是理解购买概率和弹性的简单方法。再补充两个例子：最多和最少的问题。这种方法的核心是，如果你让人们对10个功能进行排名，多数人会觉得这个过程痛苦且混乱，因为中间总有灰色地带，所有功能看起来都差不多。（00:30:06）：心理学理论表明，人们善于识别极端情况，而在中间地带时就会感到困难。因此，我们在为客户制定研发路线图时，会从10个功能中挑选出6个左右，让用户选出最重要和最不重要的功能。最重要的是“必须拥有，愿意为此付费”；最不重要的则是“不需要，绝不付费”。人们可以反复进行这种选择，然后换不同的6个功能组合继续提问。（00:30:49）：通过多次重复，你就能相对准确地排列所有功能的优先级，真正理解驱动用户付费意愿的关键因素。最后一种更高级的方法是权衡交易练习。比如，我们会让用户模拟真实的购买场景，问“如果你的软件产品有这样的包装和定价方案，你会怎么做？”这类问题更贴近现实生活，涵盖功能、价格、套餐数量等所有要素。（00:31:21）：然后我们会调整条件，继续提问。
好的。如果改变产品特性和价格，你会作何反应？你会购买这些产品中的任何一款吗？还是会说，我一个都不会选？这些更像是针对你产品的购物场景，但它很现实，也很贴近现实生活。根据人们对这些产品的选择方式，我们试图揭示人们做决策时所遵循的心理模型和规则。例如，如果我增加某些特性并提高价格，人们会说：“知道吗？我不会再买任何东西了。” （00:31:50）这实际上告诉你，增加这些特性后，人们不愿意为价格上涨买单，所以他们会退出你为客户提供的产品阵营。  
如果进行这类分析，你可以更准确地了解价格弹性，建立一些模拟模型，试图理解市场反应等。不同的方法适用于产品开发的不同阶段和公司发展的不同阶段。  
如果你还处于早期阶段，比如只是一个想法，进行初步讨论。例如，询问“你愿意为此付费吗？”是个好问题。如果有人回答“不愿意”，再追问原因。你会获得很多有价值的信息。如果有人回答“愿意”，再问“为什么愿意付费？”他们会阐述自己理解的价值，这应该纳入你的价值传达中。  
这些都是简单的问题。  
如果你处于中期阶段，比如产品开发的[00:32:44]阶段，可能需要一些购买属性问题。所有这些方法都可以快速获得初步结论或观点。  
如果你正在推出产品，处于产品或公司生命周期的后期阶段，需要更精确地制定定价和包装策略，那么一些权衡练习、最优解、全有全无等方法就变得极其重要。  
抱歉，回答得有点长，但方法实在太多了。所有这些都总结在第四章。所以只需阅读书中第四章即可。

But when you showcase the product and say, okay, this is the product that I'm building which will actually meet this need, you want to see if people's eyes slide up. And that's also when you need to have the willingness to pay conversation because it's not just about saying but actually meaning what you say. And that can only be bought in if you actually use willingness to pay in the conversation. Otherwise, it's a bit of an empty self fulfilling conversation often, so. And then when you actually do this more and more, like I said, [inaudible 00:37:00] or refining things, then you can bring this into other pieces of the conversation and gets more smarter before you launch the product.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我会把这看作……我不一定说这是用户研究。这比用户研究更早一步。用户研究可能更侧重于可用性，以及人们实际如何使用产品。这是在对话前的一步，目的是了解测试和学习情况，判断人们是否认同你的想法、是否能看到其价值、是否有投资回报率。坦白说，还要了解你真正在市场中解决了哪些需求。人们可以整天阐述他们的工作任务或需求痛点，但作为产品人员，你的职责是确定要构建的产品。当你展示产品并说，这就是我要打造的产品，能满足这些需求时，看看人们是否会眼前一亮。这时就需要进行意愿支付对话，因为光说不做是没用的。只有在对话中真正体现出意愿支付，才能让对话更有意义。否则，往往就是一场空洞的自说自话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a rule of thumb of how many people you should talk to, at least, to get a pretty good sense of maybe we've gotten some-
turns.zh: 你有没有一个经验法则，至少要和多少人交流，才能比较清楚地了解市场需求？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah, I get this question all the time, and I say, please talk to one person. [inaudible 00:37:21] because most companies are not even doing that, in terms of willingness to [inaudible 00:37:25] conversations. But if you're, let's say a B2C company, of course you have scale in terms of reaching customers. You might have hundred thousands and millions of customers, consumers. In those situations, more of a quantitative validation might be easier to run. So if you get even 1,000, 2,000 responses that could be statistically significant and easy to do and pull off. If you're a B2B SaaS company and you're focusing on let's say 20 to 30 accounts leading 80 to 90% of your business, try to talk to as many of those as possible. So at least in the 20 to 30 ballpark. And often in these conversations after a point, you start hearing stuff repeatedly. If 20 people tell you the idea is horrible, it is horrible. You can test it all you want. So when you start hearing these things, then you pivot.
turns.zh: 是的，我经常被问到这个问题。我会说，请先和一个人交流。[00:37:21不可听清]因为大多数公司甚至没有进行意愿支付对话。但如果你是一家B2C公司，当然你有客户规模优势，可能有成千上万的消费者。在这种情况下，进行量化验证可能更容易。比如收集1000到2000份反馈，就有统计意义了，也容易操作。如果你是一家B2B SaaS公司，专注于20到30个客户，占据业务的80%到90%，那就尽可能多地与这些客户交流。至少在20到30个客户的范围内。通常在对话到某个阶段后，你会反复听到同样的反馈。如果20个人告诉你这个想法很糟糕，那它确实很糟糕。你可以尽可能多地测试，但一旦你听到这些反馈，就该调整方向了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then once you have your initial thought on what pricing should be, how often do you suggest folks iterate on their pricing strategy?
turns.zh: 那么，一旦你确定了初步的定价策略，你建议人们多久迭代一次定价策略？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Yeah. Usually we say at least every six months pause, and think whether you should revisit it. Within 12 to 18 months, probably there is time to revisit, especially given market dynamics in most industry verticals that people are in today. And also, there are some pivot points where it'll make sense to think about this, like you're introducing a new plan or you're introducing some new features. All of those moments in time from a product journey standpoint would necessitate having this conversation.
turns.zh: 是的。通常我们建议至少每六个月暂停一下，重新评估是否需要调整。在12到18个月内，可能有时间重新评估，特别是考虑到当今大多数行业垂直领域的市场动态。此外，有些关键节点也需要重新思考定价策略，比如推出新套餐或新功能。从产品旅程的角度来看，这些都是需要进行这类对话的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Final question on this topic, which we've spent I think half an hour on, which is awesome, because it's probably the most important to start with, but this is going to be a deep episode. What's the first thing that a founder or PM should do to go down the route of willingness to pay, if they were to start something on Monday?
turns.zh: 明白了。关于这个话题的最后一个问题——我们已经讨论了大约半个小时，这很棒，因为这可能是最重要的入手点，但这将是一期深入探讨的节目。如果创始人或产品经理要在周一开始做一项业务，他们首先应该做什么来探索客户的支付意愿呢？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: First of all, start educating yourself that there is a science on this topic. It's not just an art. Get confidence that people have done this before. Not only just startups, but companies like Borsch, and then read chapter four and do it.
turns.zh: 首先，要认识到这个话题是有科学依据的，它不只是个艺术活。要相信之前有人做过类似的尝试。不仅是初创公司，比如Borsch这样的公司也有成功案例。建议你先通读第四章，然后付诸实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Topic two, which I know is really a big deal to you and a core part of the way you think about it in addition to willingness to pay, and it's segmentation. Thinking about how to segment your customers and product. So can you just talk about, broadly, why is this so important to think about segmentation when you're thinking about pricing?
turns.zh: 好的。第二个话题，我知道这对你来说非常重要，也是你思考定价问题时的一个核心部分，那就是客户和产品细分策略。能否大致谈谈，在考虑定价时，为什么细分客户和产品如此重要？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Look, segmentation is a topic, again, just product market fit is a well understood term for many of your listeners. When we go and ask companies, do you have a segmentation strategy, roughly about 60% would say, yeah, we have it. And then when we check it, probably 10% of them actually have a meaningful segmentation strategy. What I mean by this is, most people think of segmentation as a demographic or persona exercise or how do I position this product to different personas and things and they get it horribly wrong. Tongue in cheek, I'll give you this example. If you think about a person who's 70 plus years old, lives in a castle, incredibly wealthy in the United Kingdom, you probably think about Charles, but that also fits Ozzy Osbourne. And I would probably measure that both of them have dramatically different tastes, need different things, value things differently, and are willing to pay for things differently. (00:40:28): If you just base things on persona, you often get it wrong. Segmentation needs to be based on what customers need, what they value, and what are they willing to pay for, and how do you productize package to different segments. So the key lesson that I want your listeners to take away is, you need to be able to productize to segments. If you're trying to build a product and try to position it to different segments, you already lost the battle, because segmentation comes down to needs and understanding needs and building products based on those needs and willingness to pay. Show that you can treat your customers differently. (00:41:03): Because if you build the same product and want to treat everyone similarly and say you have a segmentation strategy, you actually don't have it. Take a simple example. If you think about the water that we drink in a fountain, it's free. In a bottle, it's $2. You put gas in it, it's $2.50. Throw it in a mini bar, it's $5. It's the same water, but it's packaged, productized differently because people have different needs. (00:41:27): I'm price conscious, I want it in a fountain, I want it to carry it around. I probably take in the bottle, I like the taste, I take gas in it, or I'm just simply ultimately lazy and I would pay the $5 to get it out of the mini bar and not go down the hotel lobby and get it for free because that's my need. If you don't understand these needs, you'll never be able to productize to those needs. So you'll just build one product and try to position it to the different needs based segments and you won't get it right for anyone. (00:41:55): And we work with all kinds of industry verticals. We have not found a single vertical where our customer, where their clients' needs are homogenous. It is heterogeneous whether you want to accept it or not. And if you accept it, then you would start getting into the heart of segmentation and say, where is that heterogeneity? How do the needs differ in the market? How does a willingness to pay differ in the market and what can I productize to different needs and willingness to pay segments, so productizing to segments, as opposed to building one and positioning it to different segments. Usually, when I walk into these companies, they'll say, "We are building a one size fits all," I would quickly correct them and say, "One size fits none." So it's a bit of that. That's why this topic is deep, because people get the definition of segmentation wrong.
turns.zh: 听着，再说一次，细分市场是很有深度的主题。但对许多听众来说，产品市场适配（product market fit）这个术语可能更容易理解。当我们去询问企业是否有细分策略时，大约60%的企业会回答“有”。但当我们深入检查时，真正拥有有效细分策略的企业可能仅占10%。我想说的是，多数人把细分市场想得过于简单，认为这只是人口统计或用户画像的练习，或者是如何将产品定位给不同用户群体。但他们往往理解错误。举个例子：如果你想到一个70多岁、住在英国城堡里、极其富有的人，你可能会想到查尔斯王子，但奥兹·奥斯本（Ozzy Osbourne）也符合这个描述。我可以证明，他们的品味、需求、价值观和支付意愿都截然不同。（00:40:28）如果只基于用户画像做产品定位，往往会出错。细分市场必须基于客户的需求、价值观和支付意愿，并为不同细分群体打造差异化产品。我希望听众能领会的关键点是：你必须能够为不同细分群体量身定制产品。如果你试图为不同细分群体打造产品却未能实现差异化定位，那你就输了。举个简单的例子：我们从喷泉免费饮用的水，与装在瓶子里卖2美元的水，加了汽油卖2.5美元，放在迷你吧卖5美元。这是同样的水，但包装和定价方式却因用户需求不同而产生差异。（00:41:27）我注重性价比，可能选择喷泉水；想随身携带，可能选择瓶装水；喜欢口感则选择汽油水；又或者纯粹图省事愿意花5美元从迷你吧取水，因为这符合我的需求。如果你不理解这些差异，就永远无法为不同需求量身定制产品。只为不同需求定位产品，却未能真正理解差异，最终会一败涂地。（00:41:55）我们服务过各种行业垂直领域，却未发现有任何行业的客户需求是完全同质化的。无论你愿不愿意承认，这种异质性都是客观存在的。如果接受这一点，你就能深入理解细分市场的核心问题：异质性体现在哪里？市场需求如何差异化？市场支付意愿如何不同？如何为不同需求和支付意愿的细分群体量身定制产品？这才是量身定制细分市场的关键所在。而不是先打造一个产品，再试图将其定位给不同细分群体。通常我进入这些公司时，他们会说“我们在打造一刀切的方案”，我会迅速纠正他们：“一刀切根本行不通。” 这就是其中的深意所在。正因如此，这个话题如此深奥，因为人们对细分市场的定义存在误解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So segments are something that people hear often and I think, like you said, understand, and to your point, they think they've done segmentation. But again, to your point, a lot of times they do it wrong. You have this framework that is really interesting, this one phrase they use, "You can act differently to help you think about whether a segment makes sense and how to think about segmentation." So can you just talk about what's a sign your segmentation is correct versus not, and maybe how to think about the framework?
turns.zh: 嗯，分割客户群体（segmentation）这个概念大家经常听说，我觉得正如你所说，大多数人都能理解这个概念。但说真的，很多公司在做分割客户群体时都做得不对。你的框架真的很有意思，他们常用的那句话是：“你可以采取不同的行动方式来判断一个客户群体是否合理，以及如何进行分割。” 能否请你详细讲讲，如何判断分割客户群体是否成功，以及如何运用这个框架？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: So the three most important words in what you said is, "You act differently," so you as in your product teams, your sales teams, your marketing teams, your finance teams, act as in, come up with new products, build a business case, come up with a product marketing messages, sales strategies, differently, as in there's no point in doing segmentation and having the same reaction or treatment to everyone. You need to be able to act differently. So what that means is, if I know what you need, what you're willing to pay for and what you value, then my conversation with you will be different than someone else who needs something else and is willing to pay something else. I productize something for Lenny, and I productize something else for the others. (00:43:53): And the key here is to understand if there is a significant, let's say, total available market or size of the market, where the needs are similar, and they're willing to pay, as in, let's try to find all the people who would want to drink water in the fountain. Let's find the people who want to bring it in a bottle. Let's find the people who want to have gas, would they pay for it. And then when you understand these segments, then you can say, "Okay, what do I build for these different segments?" And then focus on that segment when you launch the product. Have the marketing message for that segment and target that segment, as opposed to just building one thing and hoping that somehow these four groups will sort themselves out into your product. And that's the key thing.
turns.zh: 你刚才提到的三个关键词是“采取不同的行动方式”。具体来说，产品团队、销售团队、市场团队、财务团队需要采取不同的行动，比如开发新产品、制定商业案例、制定产品营销策略等。关键在于，不能对所有客户群体采取千篇一律的策略。需要根据客户的需求、支付意愿和价值观采取差异化策略。比如，如果我了解了客户的需求、支付意愿和价值观，那么与其他有不同需求、支付意愿的客户沟通时，我的策略就会不同。我会为Lenny设计不同的产品，为其他客户设计不同的产品。（00:43:53）关键在于，要判断是否存在一个庞大的细分市场，客户需求相似且愿意为此付费。比如，找到所有想从喷泉中取水的人，再找到想把水装瓶带走的人，最后看看他们是否愿意为此付费。一旦明确了这些细分市场，就可以制定针对不同细分市场的策略，并在产品上线时重点针对这些细分市场，制定针对性的营销信息和目标客户群，而不是简单地开发一个产品，然后指望四个不同群体能自动分流到你的产品中。这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When should early stage founders think about segmentation? Do you suggest it's right from the beginning, the first product should have multiple segments, or does it come later?
turns.zh: 初创公司创始人应该何时考虑客户细分？你建议从一开始就进行细分吗？还是说应该在产品开发后期再考虑？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: This is also an often asked question in the sense that as a startup, as an early stage founder, often the excuse is, "Hey, we don't have time. We're actually pulling stuff out of the wall. We need to get something out there." It's like, "Time is of the essence, so we need to build a product." And usually they would say, "Let's build just a product, which is every awesome thing that we are working on, and then we come back and revisit whether we want to build other versions, et cetera, and we don't have resources to even build multiple products." Well, that logic makes sense when you don't understand the concept of segmentation. (00:45:14): If you truly understand the concept of segmentation, you would say, you know what, as a first conversation, when you're having that willingness to pay conversation based on your idea, you would say, "Who's actually willing to pay for this innovation? What do they need? How many of them are there? Can we productize to this first compared to the others? "Then you'll start prioritizing not only your R&D roadmap, but you're resourcing to say, "Which segment should I start with? And then what segments would I actually add?" (00:45:40): And then your value messaging would be tailored to that segment. People will understand the benefits. They will say, "Your product will be launched and people will get it and they would actually go for it." So having done this exercise early will tell you how many segments are there, what is the size of these segments, how to prioritize them, which one to pick first and which product to build first for that segment, and then productize to the other segments later. If you're lazy and sloppy, you'll build a product, you'll slap on a price, you'll throw it in the market and say, "I will attract everyone." You'll attract no one.
turns.zh: 这也是一个常被问到的问题。作为初创公司、处于早期阶段的创始人，他们常以"我们没时间了，实际上我们正在临时拼凑产品，需要尽快推向市场"为借口。仿佛"时间就是金钱，所以我们必须先打造产品"。但通常他们会说："先把产品做出来，把我们正在研发的所有牛逼功能都塞进去，之后再回头考虑是否要开发其他版本，反正我们没资源同时开发多个产品。" 好吧，当你不理解细分市场概念时，这种逻辑倒也说得通。（00:45:14）但如果你真正理解了细分市场的概念，你会说："在基于创意进行意愿支付评估的初期对话中，我们应该问：谁愿意为这项创新买单？他们的需求是什么？目标人群规模有多大？相较于其他人群，我们能否先针对这部分群体进行产品化？" 这样一来，你不仅能合理规划研发路线图，还能合理分配资源："我该从哪个细分市场入手？然后再逐步拓展其他细分市场？" （00:45:40）随后，针对该细分市场定制价值主张。用户会明白其益处，他们会说："产品一上线，人们就会买单，肯定会追捧的。" 早期做好这项分析，能明确细分市场数量、规模，合理排序，确定首发细分市场及对应产品，再逐步向其他细分市场推广。若你偷懒敷衍，只会仓促上线产品，随便定价，投放市场后还说："我要吸引所有人"，结果必将一败涂地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So basically understand the segments right from the beginning. Don't necessarily launch products for every segment.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以关键是从一开始就搞清楚细分市场。没必要为每个细分市场都推出产品。

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Exactly. That's totally acceptable because it's not like everyone has resourcing to launch five products, five segments, everything else. Complexity, and plus, you don't probably want to be too complex when you're launching your products, but focus on the right segment, and launch it for that first.
turns.zh: 完全正确。这完全可以接受，毕竟不是每个人都有资源同时开发五款产品、覆盖五个细分市场。复杂性很高，而且在产品发布初期没必要太复杂，专注于正确的细分市场，先把它做好。

turns.zh: 是啊，我老是收到Peter的推送。说真的，我很喜欢这个产品。8美元一罐的水瓶设计很棒。肯定有不少消费者喜欢这种创意产品。

或许我会先举几个显而易见且广为人知的例子，这样大家至少能记住要点，如果有需要，我们再深入探讨。但以苹果为例，如果当初苹果的决策者是这样想的：“嘿，我们只需开发一款产品——iPhone，就能最大化市场份额，然后把它推向市场，定个高价，指望能占据市场份额。” 那如今苹果就不可能成为全球最赚钱的公司。他们实际是怎么做的呢？iPhone有299美元、399美元、499美元等不同价位，甚至高达1499美元。他们针对不同消费群体开发了多款产品。（00:49:01）我记得iPhone X发布时去苹果专卖店体验，心里不舍得花上千美元。当时我仔细查看功能，发现自己对视网膜屏等高级配置并不感兴趣。结果发现799美元的8S款同样优秀，最终就选了这款。可见我属于那个消费群体，而非iPhone X的目标用户。这就是根据不同需求细分产品线的高明之处。深入剖析会发现苹果不仅定价策略精准，更是针对不同价格区间和消费意愿进行了差异化设计，这才是其商业智慧的精髓所在。

再举个例子——我们曾合作过的B2B SaaS公司Eventbrite。在上市前期，他们推出的单一产品——

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: A SaaS company, they used to have one product that was actually servicing all of their customers. And then we went through an exercise of understanding who are their customer segments and how do we productize to different segment needs. And if you look at what they have today, they have three plans, because there are segments behind this. And if you look at the plans, there are plans, for instance, the entry level plan has something like, you can only launch an event with one ticket type, like a general admission. And then if you take the middle plan, it has unlimited entry type. So you can have a general admission, a VIP admission, whatever, when you're actually having events. It actually makes sense, because if you're, let's say, hosting your local wine club meetup, whatever, event, you probably just need the general admission and that's it. But if you actually are a bit more professional and you needed multiple event types and you're having a event of that nature, then there's another product that actually appeals. (00:50:57): But because of doing this, the one that has only one event type, that product is cheaper than the other one. So there's an essential product and there's a professional product and they have enterprise product. So this comes down to truly understanding what customers need, what they value, and what they're willing to pay for, and how can we productize towards that. Maybe another example that is obvious and in front of us, when we use our apps, like Uber is a great example of also segmentation.Because you have different car types. If they just had one car type, then okay, then that's a very different company, very different strategy. There's an Uber Black, Uber X. We used to even have the Uber pool pre pandemic. I don't know if it's back now.
turns.zh:
有一家SaaS公司，过去他们只有一款产品为所有客户提供服务。但后来我们通过一系列分析，明确了客户的不同细分群体，并针对不同需求开发产品。如今该公司推出了三种套餐方案，这背后正是基于客户细分的考量。以入门级套餐为例，用户只能设置一种门票类型，比如普通入场券；而中级套餐则支持无限种类门票，包括普通票、VIP票等。这设计得很合理——比如举办本地葡萄酒俱乐部聚会时，可能只需要普通票；但如果活动更专业，需要多种票种，那中级套餐就能满足需求。

（00:50:57）由于这种差异化策略，单一门票类型的套餐价格比其他套餐更低。这里体现了核心产品与专业产品的差异化定位，同时兼顾企业级解决方案。关键在于深刻理解客户需求、价值诉求和支付意愿，并据此设计产品。另一个显而易见的例子是Uber的差异化服务——不同车型对应不同客户群体。如果只有一种车型，公司战略将完全不同。Uber曾推出“Uber Black”、“Uber X”服务，疫情前甚至有“Uber Pool”拼车选项，目前尚不确定是否恢复。

turns.en: I think it's back.

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: It's back? Great. And they also launched this thing called comfort, which is a bit between Black and Uber X in terms of both price and also the types of cars. (00:51:46): But it comes with certain features. For instance, you can say quiet preferred on a Comfort or a Black. And that's literally why I take one of these, because I'm probably working on my Uber ride over and I like to just have the quiet and just work on things, and I'm willing to pay for that and I belong in a different segment. But of course if I'm using, let's say Uber for my everyday commute, sometime maybe I do pool. So depending on even my point in time or depending on my situation, I might actually belong to different segments, and understanding this and then productizing towards that becomes key. (00:52:24): So the topic that we have been focused with many companies nowadays is not just doing a static view of segmentation, but truly understanding dynamic segmentation and how to offer product and services around the fact that people switch segments. So if I'm ordering on a Friday night on a food delivery platform, maybe I'm thinking pizza. Tuesday afternoon during my office time, maybe I'm thinking of a different type of cuisine. So if I know all of these things, healthy choices versus not, when can I productize what, then you actually start getting a dynamic views of segmentation. And the technology around us actually allows us to take a very dynamic view of segments and that's very fascinating. So the [inaudible 00:53:09] there are multiple steps. First do the segmentation, that's the basic. [inaudible 00:53:14] a static view. Maybe if it's relevant, even a dynamic view of this is the next frontier.
turns.zh:
它又回来了？太好了。他们还推出了名为"Comfort"的服务，在价格和车型方面介于Black和Uber X之间。（00:51:46）不过它有一些特别的功能。比如，你可以在Comfort或Black订单中选择"安静优先"模式。这正是我选择这种服务的原因——因为我可能正在车上处理工作，需要安静的环境专注工作，所以我愿意为此付费，也属于不同的服务层级。但当然，如果我日常通勤用Uber，有时也会拼车。所以根据不同时间段或实际情况，我可能需要切换到不同服务层级。理解并据此调整产品策略至关重要。

（00:52:24）如今许多公司关注的焦点，不只是静态的细分分析，而是要深入理解动态细分，以及如何根据用户的服务切换行为提供产品和服务。比如周五晚上在外卖平台下单，可能选择披萨；周二下午在办公室，可能想换种口味。若能掌握这些用户行为特征——比如健康饮食偏好、使用场景——就能构建动态细分模型。而科技的发展让这类细分分析变得更加可行，这实在令人着迷。

[00:53:09未听清]细分分析有多个步骤。首先是静态分析，必要时再进行动态分析，动态分析是下一个前沿领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which you shared just now reminded me of another really interesting framework in your book, around pricing strategy. And you talk a lot about just how important it is, one to just write down your strategy and why you think this is the right strategy. But specifically, you have these concepts of either you want to be maximizing, you want to be penetrating or you want to be skimming. And I thought this would be a good time to chat a little bit about that. Can you just talk about what these three strategies are?
turns.zh: 你刚才提到的内容让我想起你书中另一个非常有趣的定价策略框架。你多次强调，制定策略并阐明其合理性至关重要。具体来说，你提到了三种策略：最大化定价、渗透定价和抽水定价。我觉得现在是个好机会，咱们可以深入探讨一下这三种策略。你能简单讲讲它们各自的含义吗？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: Sure. When we talk about pricing strategies, we hear many buzzwords, and it's irrelevant. So when we take a step back and look at it, there's literally only three types of pricing strategies. And if you know this, then you can follow one of these and [inaudible 00:53:57] to success products. The first one is skimming strategy, which is your Apple iPhone. They launch at a particular price and the next generation is probably at a higher price, but the previous generation actually goes down, so they launch at a higher price and then they start lowering the price. So they're skimming the market. And connotation of these products is also, it's a premium product. Price is a signal of quality, et cetera, et cetera. (00:54:20): If you take penetration that's probably made famous by Amazon. And Amazon, they're probably operating at much thinner margins, but they're playing the volume game. Much more harder game to play because you need to have all of your costs in order, supply chain, everything else, and you're fine tuning towards the volume game. Often, I see entrepreneurs who say, "Let's just price load to gain growth." That's a fallacy. If you don't have a business model that actually supports this compared to Amazon, then you probably shouldn't be in a penetration strategy. And even in a company like Amazon and AWS has a very different strategy compared to the e-commerce marketplace. So within even business units, you can actually have different pricing strategies. (00:55:01): And the third one is just maximization, which is you're neither on these two extremes but a bit in between, and you're saying, "Okay, what can I maximize in the next couple of years?" In my opinion at least Microsoft will probably belong in that category. And if I look at Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, companies that reached trillion valuations in our lifetime, probably the only three in some way, shape or form, they have dramatically different pricing strategies. The point is not about picking, just picking one, but it's about executing the one that you actually pick. And that's also what we write about in the book, how to pick one and not just pick one, but how to build your products around this executed live and breathe your business model strategy, which leads to your pricing strategy.
turns.zh: 好的。当我们谈论定价策略时，会听到很多术语，但这些术语其实并没有什么实际意义。所以退一步来看，其实定价策略只有三种类型。只要你了解了这些，就能选择其中一种，并[此处语音不清]成功打造出爆款产品。第一种是撇脂定价策略，以苹果iPhone为例。他们以特定价格推出新品，次代产品价格可能更高，但前代产品价格却会下调——先高价上市，再降价销售。这就是典型的撇脂定价策略。这种产品通常被赋予高端形象，价格被视为质量的象征等（00:54:20）。如果谈到渗透定价，可能最著名的例子就是亚马逊。亚马逊的利润率可能更低，但他们走的是量大价低的路线。这条路更难走，因为你需要把所有成本控制到位，供应链等各方面都做到位，然后才能专注于量大价低的策略。我经常看到创业者说：“我们就加价销售来获取增长。”这是一个误区。如果你的商业模式无法与亚马逊抗衡，那你就不该采用渗透定价策略。即使像亚马逊和AWS这样的公司，其策略也与电商平台有很大不同。因此，即使在同一公司内部，不同业务部门也可能采用不同的定价策略。（00:55:01）第三种是最大化定价策略，即不偏不倚，介于两者之间。你会问：“未来几年我能如何实现利润最大化？”至少在我看来，微软可能属于这一类。看看苹果、微软、亚马逊这些在我们有生之年估值达到万亿美元的公司，几乎只有这三家在某种程度上采用了截然不同的定价策略。关键不在于选择一种策略，而是要执行你选择的策略。这也是我们在书中强调的——如何选择策略，并不仅仅是选定一种，而是要围绕所选策略打造产品，真正践行你的商业模式策略，最终落到定价策略上。

turns.en: Amazing. I just want to say I love how deep we're getting into all these topics. This is amazing.

You talk a lot about the importance of packaging and bundling and how that alone can help you win a segment, versus even the price of the segment. Can you talk about how to think about the importance of that?
turns.zh: 关于这个话题的最后一个问题，然后我们就进入下一个话题，剩下的部分会更快。我们在每个话题上花了很多时间，我很喜欢这样。你多次强调包装和捆绑销售的重要性，以及仅靠这些就能帮助你赢得某个细分市场，甚至超过该细分市场的价格。你能谈谈如何理解这一点的重要性吗？

turns.speaker: Madhavan Ramanujam
turns.en: The way to unlock your segmentation is to think about bundling and packaging, as in you're configuring your product, based on what customers need, what they value and what they're willing to pay for. Either you put a bunch of benefits that people like and call it packaging and put that out, or you're taking multiple products and calling it bundling and putting that out. So it's a question of, hey, that's the way you unlock segments. Your productizing. It's like the iPhone X versus the iPhone A test, different products, different features, different packages, et cetera. (00:56:36): The quick framework to think about packaging, bundling, we call it the leaders, fillers and killers, exercise of framework. So if you think about the classic, let's say bundle, like a Big Mac or a Happy Meal, the Big Mac is the leader product, that's in the Happy Meal, and that's what people go for when they go to McDonald's. When you look at french fries and Coke, those are the fillers. You can put a burger along with french fries and coke, call it a happy meal, and most people wouldn't have bought a french fry or Coke, but if you just say for a dollar or two more, you know can actually get this, they would say, "Let's get the happy Meal." So you're actually bundling it in such a way that with marginal increase in price, you're also able to sell multiple products, which they wouldn't have if you didn't have it. (00:57:22): The killer is the one where if you put it in the product, it just kills the bundle for everyone. So for instance, if you put coffee along with french fries and a coke and a burger, that's just going to kill the bundle. No one needs a double dose of caffeine when they're having a burger. But there are people like me, Lenny, who love to have coffee with their burgers. So these are great candidates for selling them as add-ons, because if I actually, I would pay for the add-on because I actually want the coffee. So I would take the burgers standalone, and I would take the coffee standalone and that's why it's actually listed separately in the menus. (00:57:56): If you bundle it, what happens is it just depreciates the willingness to pay across the entire customer base to the point where no one actually wants it. So you need to find pockets of customers who want it and then maybe only sell it to them. So the rule of thumb that I usually say is, if 10 to 20% of your customers want something and they really want it badly, that's usually an add-on. That's not something that goes into a package unless you have a advanced package just for them, kind of thing. And if more than 50% of people want something, that's a leader product. So if you understand all these leaders, fillers and killers, then you can configure your product in such a way that your productizing to segments and you'll unlock maximum value.
turns.zh:
解锁细分市场的关键在于思考产品打包与捆绑策略。具体而言，就是根据客户需求、价值取向和支付意愿来配置产品。或者你可以整合一系列受众喜爱的权益并将其打包推出；又或者将多款产品组合在一起形成捆绑套餐。关键在于，如何通过这种方式精准锁定目标客户群体，并释放产品最大价值。

（00:56:36）：思考产品打包与捆绑的快速框架，我们称之为“领头者、填充者与杀手”练习。以经典的套餐组合为例，比如麦当劳的开心乐园餐。汉堡是核心产品，包含在套餐中，也是消费者光顾麦当劳的主要诉求。薯条和可乐则属于填充产品。若将汉堡与薯条、可乐捆绑销售，大多数人可能不会单独购买薯条或可乐，但只要加价一两美元，就能促使他们选择套餐。这种微增价策略能有效捆绑多款产品，否则单独销售可能面临市场冷淡。

（00:57:22）：杀手产品指的是当你将其加入套餐时，会直接破坏整个捆绑组合的价值。例如，若在汉堡套餐中加入咖啡，多数人会觉得多余，因为吃汉堡时没必要摄入过多咖啡因。但像我这样喜欢边吃汉堡边喝咖啡的人，就乐意将其作为附加产品购买。正因如此，菜单上会单独列出咖啡和汉堡的价格。若将它们捆绑销售，反而会降低整体客户支付意愿，导致无人问津。

（00:57:56）：若捆绑产品会降低整体客户支付意愿，那么就需要精准定位目标客户群体，仅向特定人群销售。我的经验法则是：当10%至20%的客户强烈需求某种产品时，通常可以作为附加产品；除非为特定人群设计高级套餐，否则不应将其纳入基础套餐。若超过50%的客户对某种产品感兴趣，那它就是领头产品。

The ones that are nice to have and might consider paying or nice to have, those features are probably the fillers, and that don't need are the killers.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。所以当你把最常用和最不常用的功能按重要性排序时，那些必须具备的功能才会收费，或者说必须具备的核心功能、特性或优势才会成为主推产品。那些可有可无、可能考虑付费的功能，可能是填充性内容，而那些根本不需要的功能则堪称"致命缺陷"。
